name: Pop
blurb: From the Wall of Sound to the streaming age: sixty years of songs everyone knows.

stories.title: Good Vibrations
stories.dek: A pocket symphony built from pieces
stories.body:
By 1966 Brian Wilson was no longer touring with the Beach Boys. The band was on the road playing surf and car songs while he stayed home in California writing and producing. After the album Pet Sounds, he wanted to make something even more ambitious: a single that would be a small symphony.

He later said the idea came from his mother, who once told him that dogs bark at some people because they can sense their vibrations. The thought stuck. Wilson began to write a song about feelings that could be felt but not seen, and he decided to make the recording in pieces. Over several months he worked at studios across Los Angeles, including Gold Star, Western and Columbia. At each one he recorded a different section of music with the Los Angeles studio players sometimes called the Wrecking Crew. Each studio had its own sound, and Wilson used that to his advantage.

The recording included cellos, organ and an unusual instrument called the electro-theremin. It was not a true theremin, but it produced a similar sweeping, eerie whistle. The musician who played it, Paul Tanner, was a former trombonist from the Glenn Miller orchestra who had helped design the device. That sound became the song's hook and gave listeners a strange, thrilling shiver.

Wilson then edited the sections together on tape into a three-and-a-half-minute record. Mike Love wrote the final lyrics. The cost of the recording was reportedly enormous for a single in that era. When Capitol Records released it in October 1966, the song soared to the top of the charts in both the United States and Britain.

For Wilson, it should have been a triumph. He began work on a larger album, called Smile, which was meant to build on the same ideas. But the project proved difficult. The band argued, Wilson grew anxious, and the recording was shelved in 1967. For decades the music circulated only among fans. Wilson finally completed a new version in 2004, and the original sessions were released in 2011 as The Smile Sessions.

"Good Vibrations" remained the single piece that showed what he had been aiming for. It proved that a pop record could be built like a film score, from many small parts, and that a three-minute song could be as daring as anything in rock.

stories.title: ABBA
stories.dek: From Eurovision to a worldwide sound
stories.body:
In the early 1970s two Swedish songwriters, Björn Ulvaeus and Benny Andersson, were looking for a way to become known outside their country. Each had been in a popular band at home. They met in 1966 and began writing together. Björn married a singer, Agnetha Fältskog, in 1971, and Benny was with another singer, Anni-Frid Lyngstad, known as Frida. The four were two couples, and they began recording together.

Their manager, Stig Anderson, saw a way forward in the Eurovision Song Contest, a televised event watched across Europe. In 1973 they entered a song and finished third in the Swedish selection. A year later they tried again with "Waterloo", a rousing song with a thumping beat. On April 6, 1974, in Brighton, England, the group appeared in glittery costumes and won. Eurovision had rarely launched a career this large, and the song became a hit across Europe.

ABBA, a name made from the initials of their first names, then went on a remarkable run. They recorded in Stockholm, and later at their own Polar Studios. They wrote their own songs, with Björn on lyrics and Benny on music, and they spent weeks perfecting a sound of layered voices, bright keyboards and a clear, polished mix.

In June 1976 they performed a new song, "Dancing Queen," on a television gala in Stockholm on the eve of the wedding of King Carl XVI Gustaf and Silvia Sommerlath. It was a soaring song with a classic piano opening. It became one of the group's best-known recordings, and it remains a staple of dance floors and weddings.

The group's songs grew more emotional as the years passed. Both marriages ended, and their lives were in the public eye. Yet they continued to release strong work, including the album Super Trouper in 1980, until the group stopped working together in the early 1980s.

Interest in the music never faded. In 1999 a stage musical, Mamma Mia!, put their songs into a new story. It ran for years in London and around the world and later became a hit film. A group that began as an entry in a song contest had become part of the world's shared pop memory.

stories.title: Elton John and Bernie Taupin
stories.dek: Two strangers, one envelope of lyrics
stories.body:
In 1967 two young men answered the same advertisement in a British music paper. Liberty Records was looking for new songwriters. One was Reginald Dwight, a piano player from the London suburbs who had been playing in a band and had a gift for melody. The other was Bernie Taupin, a teenager from Lincolnshire who wrote verses about the American West but had no music. The label's talent scout saw that they were a perfect match, though neither had met the other.

They began to work together by mail. Taupin would write lyrics and send them to Dwight, who by then was calling himself Elton John, and Elton would set them to music. That was how they worked for decades. They seldom wrote in the same room. According to a story that John has often told, he wrote the tune for "Your Song" in about twenty minutes.

Success came in 1970. In August Elton John played his first American show at the Troubadour in Los Angeles. Before an audience that included music-industry people he pounded the piano, leapt around the stage and sang with an energy that few had expected. The next morning, reviews called him a star. His album Elton John and its single "Your Song" were hits.

A string of albums followed. Honky Château in 1972 included "Rocket Man," a song that Taupin has said was inspired by a Ray Bradbury story. Goodbye Yellow Brick Road in 1973 included "Candle in the Wind," Taupin's tribute to Marilyn Monroe. In the mid-1970s John was among the biggest stars in the world, known for oversized glasses and feathered costumes.

The partnership continued to produce hits. In 1997, after the death of Princess Diana, Taupin rewrote the words of "Candle in the Wind" for her funeral, and Elton sang it at Westminster Abbey. The record was among the best-selling singles of all time.

The two men remained friends and collaborators for more than fifty years. The pairing remains one of the most successful songwriting partnerships in popular music.
